data.title: Can smarter technology selection help de-risk small-molecule development?
data.description:
For a small-molecule drug candidate, a compound must dissolve, reach the required exposure, remain stable and be manufactured consistently at progressively larger scales, but these requirements are becoming harder to reconcile as development pipelines include increasingly complex molecules.  

Adding to the challenge, the consequences often emerge only after formulation work or pharmacokinetic studies have begun. At that point, the remedy may involve a new formulation, additional clinical or preclinical work, or redevelopment of the manufacturing process. 

Avoiding this cycle requires selecting technology based on the molecule’s dominant limitation and staying informed by the requirements of the eventual product. An approach that improves exposure but creates an unstable intermediate, an expensive process or an impractical dosage form can simply transfer risk to a later development stage, but predictive development can help teams make these decisions earlier. 

Fewer, more informed experiments allow teams to test the most promising pathways before committing large amounts of active pharmaceutical ingredient (API) and significant development time. The goal is to reduce the formulation options while ensuring stability, manufacturability, and downstream needs are considered. 

Identifying developability problems 

The first step is to build a detailed picture of the API against the target product profile. The intended dose, solubility under relevant intestinal conditions, and permeability help establish whether dissolution rate, intestinal solubility or membrane transport is the main barrier. Stability and solid-state behaviour then inform which interventions are feasible. 

The developability classification system (DCS) can help determine whether absorption is primarily limited by dissolution, solubility or permeability. That distinction is significant because compounds with seemingly similar bioavailability problems may require very different interventions. 

The key issue is what prevents the intended dose from reaching the necessary exposure levels: Does the compound dissolve too slowly, is it insufficiently soluble under intestinal conditions, or is transport across the intestinal membrane the main barrier? Dissolution and solubility measurements under relevant conditions, permeability assessment and solid-state characterisation can help distinguish these mechanisms. The precipitation following dissolution also requires careful consideration, as an early rise in dissolved drug levels may not last long enough to facilitate absorption. Poor solubility does not automatically mean an amorphous solid dispersion (ASD) is the solution, but selecting a technology without identifying the rate-limiting mechanism risks solving the wrong problem. 

Choosing a formulation when several constraints apply 

A molecule may simultaneously exhibit poor solubility, limited permeability, and sensitivity to heat or moisture. Teams should determine which of these factors most significantly restricts exposure at the planned dose, then evaluate if solving that issue would leave other barriers still preventing the product from hitting its target. The primary limitation serves as a hypothesis to test and update as new evidence emerges. 

Candidate approaches should be evaluated based on the same product requirements. Improving dissolution alone offers limited benefit if permeability continues to restrict absorption. Likewise, a positive exposure profile is insufficient if achieving the necessary drug loading results in an impractically large tablet or the formulation fails to stay stable during storage. The best approach is to target the key limiting mechanism within a feasible development and manufacturing process. 
 
For example, micronisation or nanomilling may be appropriate when the dissolution rate is the main constraint, as smaller particles provide greater surface area for dissolution. If the amount that can dissolve remains as inadequate at the intended dose, particle-size reduction alone may be insufficient. Salt selection or ASD may then merit investigation, depending on the compound and its solid-state properties. 

By maintaining the API in a higher-energy amorphous state within a polymer matrix, an ASD can improve apparent solubility and dissolution. That benefit must be weighed against physical stability and the ability to maintain the required performance. Lipid-based formulations offer another option for suitable lipophilic compounds, but their capacity to carry the dose and maintain drug in solution after dilution or digestion needs evaluation. 

The benefits of predictive development 

Thermo Fisher Scientific is increasingly using predictive modelling to support this diagnostic stage. Its OSDPredict™ digital toolbox incorporates Quadrant 2, an artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning-enabled platform designed to predict formulation behaviour using information about a compound’s molecular structure and chemical characteristics alongside the target product profile. Quadrant 2 applies several computational approaches, including molecular dynamics, quantitative structure-activity relationship (QSAR) modelling and absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion and toxicity (ADMET) analysis. The aim is to narrow the range of potentially viable formulation strategies before scarce API is consumed in extensive experimental screening. 

Predictive tools can also inform the wider development strategy. Absorption modelling can assess whether an anticipated improvement in dissolution is likely to translate into exposure, while stability prediction and process modelling can flag risks that affect a formulation’s usefulness beyond its initial performance. 

However, these tools do not eliminate experimental development. Predictions depend on available inputs and model applicability, so shortlisted approaches still require experimental confirmation. The resulting studies should resolve specific uncertainties, including whether a formulation sustains its performance and whether the proposed process is feasible. New data can then refine the next development decision. 

Assessing stability and scale   

Selecting an ASD does not settle the manufacturing route. Spray drying, for example, can be attractive early in development because feasibility studies can be conducted with relatively small API quantities. However, it requires the drug and polymer to be soluble in an appropriate solvent system. A process built around very low solids content can also become expensive at commercial volumes, potentially creating a cost-of-goods problem that was not apparent during early development. Teams should investigate that cost and capacity burden before it becomes embedded in the process. 

Hot-melt extrusion (HME) offers an alternative for compatible compounds. It is typically a solvent-free continuous process and can offer commercial advantages, but the API and polymer must tolerate the heat and shear involved. 

The decision needs to account for drug-polymer compatibility, achievable drug loading, chemical and physical stability, solvent requirements, downstream processing and eventual scale. The intended final dosage form should also be considered, as an intermediate that performs well immediately after spray drying or extrusion still needs to be developed into a robust tablet, capsule or other finished product. 

Thinking through those downstream steps at the outset can prevent a Phase I solution from becoming a Phase III manufacturing bottleneck. 

Making early decisions with the final product in view 

The goal should be a development strategy that is phase-appropriate without becoming phase-limited. A powder-in-bottle presentation may be perfectly reasonable for an early clinical study, for example, but teams should already understand how the formulation and process could evolve towards a scalable commercial product. Early decisions should document why the route was selected, which constraints remain unresolved, and what evidence would trigger reconsideration.  

For a promising laboratory formulation, this means identifying the next studies needed to establish stability, practical drug loading, and process feasibility. It also means understanding the implications of a later formulation change before clinical supply, and manufacturing plans depend on the initial choice. 

ThermoFisher’s OSDPredict platform is intended to connect these predictive tools across areas including bioperformance, stability and manufacturability, and its value is not simply in the availability of multiple modelling tools. Instead, it is its ability to narrow the formulation space earlier, prioritise more promising approaches, and focus experimental work where it is most informative.

data.title: OrbiMed raises $3bn to back global life science players
data.description:
Global healthcare investment giant OrbiMed has raised $3bn for two new private equity funds to support the growth of companies across the European, US and Asian life sciences sectors. 

This raise has seen OrbiMed establish two new funds. The first, dubbed OrbiMed Private Investments X, has raised over $1.9bn to siphon cash into both US and European life sciences venture capital opportunities. 

Meanwhile, the second private equity fund, OrbiMed Asia Partners VI, has raised over $1bn, which will support Asian companies by investing in venture capital and healthcare growth opportunities across the continent. 

Coming three years after the launch of their previous iterations, the latest tranches will support companies across a broad spectrum of disciplines within the life sciences sector, though the primary investment focus will lie in the realm of biopharmaceuticals, as well as technology-enabled healthcare services, medical devices and diagnostics. 

The investors behind these new funds, OrbiMed says, come from broad sources, with medical institutions, pension funds, family offices, sovereign wealth funds and university endowments all contributing a portion of the capital to this raise. 

According to OrbiMed’s managing partner, Carl Gordon, there has never been a more exciting time to be investing in life sciences. “AI, a proliferation of new therapeutic modalities and China’s emergence as a biotechnology powerhouse are expanding the opportunities to develop transformative treatments,” Gordon commented.  

“We look forward to helping entrepreneurs turn these advances into leading healthcare companies.”   

OrbiMed’s most recent raise follows a similar tack to fellow healthcare investor ARCH Venture Partners, which detailed plans for a $3bn raise to support early-stage biotech in August 2026. 

Meanwhile, Europe’s largest life sciences-dedicated venture capital firm, Forbion, also raised €2.3bn ($2.6bn) across two funds earlier this month, which will support around 30 “high-potential” biotech companies. 

However, a recent report from GlobalData, the parent company of Pharmaceutical Technology, revealed that the value and volume of global venture capital investments both dropped quarter-on-quarter (QoQ) in Q3 2026 compared with Q2. The Asia Pacific Region (APAC), driven by China, bucked the trend, with the value of deals across the region growing by 20.7% QoQ.

data.title: AstraZeneca and insitro forge $1.5bn AI-powered cardiometabolic partnership
data.description:
AstraZeneca has inked a billion-dollar artificial intelligence (AI)-powered drug discovery partnership and licensing deal with insitro, to identify novel targets and therapies for a range of cardiometabolic diseases. 

Through this partnership, the pair will focus on creating drugs to fulfil unmet needs and address the underlying drivers of disease in both metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) and heart muscle-impacting cardiomyopathies. 

In exchange for an upfront payment of $40m and around $1.46bn in potential development and commercial milestones, AstraZeneca will secure the exclusive global rights to develop selected programmes developed through this partnership. The UK-Swedish pharma giant will also award insitro single-digit royalties on global sales of the fruits of this collaboration, provided they make it to market. 

At the heart of this partnership is insitro’s Virtual Human AI platform trained on large-scale human and cellular data, which the biotech uses to identify causal disease biology.  

According to insitro’s founder and CEO, Daphne Koller, applying AI to complex datasets around MASH and cardiomyopathies can allow the pair to “unlock greater discovery power” and reveal new insights into the genetics behind such diseases.  

“Our platform simultaneously deconvolutes disease biology and identifies causal drivers of disease pathologies,” Koller commented, adding that pairing expertise with AstraZeneca will allow the duo to scale with the potential to more rapidly progress novel programmes through the development stages to patients.  

AstraZeneca targets increasingly lucrative MASH arena

AstraZeneca forges its collaboration as the company looks to deepen its legacy in the cardiovascular, renal and metabolic (CVRM) segment. Currently, the pharma giant has a plethora of marketed medicines in this disease area – including blockbuster SGLT2 inhibitor, Farxiga (dapagliflozin), which is now subject to generic erosion due to its US loss of market exclusivity earlier this year. 

It also marks a doubling down on AstraZeneca’s intent to enter the MASH market, as it is currently exploring the potential of a small molecule FAP inhibitor, AZD2389, in Phase II trials. The company hopes it will demonstrate better efficacy than its former antisense oligonucleotide MASH candidate, AZD2693, which it scrapped after it produced lacklustre results in a Phase II study. 

AstraZeneca makes moves toward the MASH market as it becomes increasingly lucrative, with a recent report from GlobalData, parent company of Pharmaceutical Technology, forecasting that the segment will balloon from a value of $802.3m in 2022 at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 38.2% to a value of $20.3bn by 2032. 

This growth, analysts say, will primarily be fuelled by the anticipated launch of several pipeline candidates and uptake of established drugs such as Madrigal Pharmaceutical’s first-to-market Rezdiffra (resmetirom) and Novo’s blockbuster glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1RA) therapy, Wegovy (semaglutide), as well as an anticipated uptick in the use of non-invasive tests for diagnosing and managing the disease. 

With this shifting MASH landscape, GlobalData analysts also point to burgeoning competition in this space, the flames of which are stoked by the potential emergence of further incretin therapies and alternative investigational antifibrotics on the market.

data.title: Acta Pharmaceuticals raises $24m for Alzheimer’s therapies
data.description:
Acta Pharmaceuticals has secured $24m in seed funding for advancing a drug pipeline focused on early intervention and prevention of Alzheimer’s disease (AD), including the clinical progression of its lead candidate, GSM-779690T.

It is a gamma-secretase modulator being developed as a potent once-daily oral therapy for the treatment and potential prevention of AD.

According to the company, existing therapies approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) either treat symptoms or clear amyloid beta (Aβ) after senile plaques accumulate.

In contrast, gamma-secretase modulators alter protein production before plaques form.

GSM-779690T lowers plaque-forming Aβ42 while boosting shorter peptides, Aβ37 and Aβ38, which impede plaque build-up.

Earlier gamma-secretase inhibitors interrupted overall enzyme activity, whereas modulators preserve normal biological functions.

Acta Pharmaceuticals expects to begin a Phase I clinical trial in October 2026 for its lead asset, GSM-779690T.

The placebo-controlled, randomised, double-blind study will assess single and multiple ascending doses in healthy adult participants.

Researchers will examine the oral small-molecule candidate’s tolerability, pharmacokinetics, and safety.

GSM-779690T remains an investigational therapy that lacks regulatory approval, with its safety and efficacy not yet established.

Acta Pharmaceuticals co-founder and CEO George Alex said: “We founded Acta Pharmaceuticals to translate more than four decades of Dr Rudolph Tanzi’s discoveries into new Alzheimer’s disease treatments to enable early intervention and prevention.

“GSM-779690T is the culmination of 25 years of research at Massachusetts General Hospital and the University of California, San Diego and approximately $70m in preclinical development funding.

“We’re privileged to build on Drs Tanzi and Wagner’s pioneering GSM research and decades of discoveries to give the broadest group of people the opportunity for early prevention and treatment of one of the world’s most devastating and costly diseases.”

Acta Pharmaceuticals is also progressing a combination therapies programme using intellectual property licensed from Massachusetts General Hospital.

The approach applies human brain cell models known as Alzheimer’s-in-a-Dish, which simulate disease features to screen hundreds of compounds simultaneously within six weeks.

Backers in the funding round include Gamma Bio Investors, Dolby Family Ventures, Alzheimer’s Disease Research Foundation, and multiple family offices and investors.

data.title: Transcripta Bio, Mayo Clinic join force on ALS therapies
data.description:
Transcripta Bio has entered into a research collaboration and licensing agreement with Mayo Clinic to identify potential treatments and therapeutic targets for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).

The initiative centres on creating a high-resolution, patient-derived molecular map of the fatal neurodegenerative disorder, which currently has few effective therapies.

Under the terms of the agreement, Mayo Clinic is prospectively recruiting living ALS patients through an Institutional Review Board-approved protocol.

The study group includes individuals with sporadic ALS as well as familial forms of the disease, spanning genetic profiles such as chromosome 9 open reading frame 72 (C9orf72), fused in sarcoma (FUS), superoxide dismutase 1 (SOD1), and TAR DNA-binding protein (TARDBP).

Donated patient tissue will undergo single-cell RNA sequencing and be evaluated alongside anonymised clinical information, including age at onset, disease duration, progression rates, genetic status, and prescribed medications.

Transcripta Bio plans to apply its transcriptomic drug-discovery platform to the tissue samples to generate patient-derived disease profiles.

By comparing these signatures against its existing drug-response data, the company seeks to nominate new intervention targets and prospective drug candidates.

The work aims to elucidate how ALS biology varies across individual patients and throughout disease progression, while generating findings that could inform patient care and accelerate the development of targeted therapies.

Transcripta Bio founder and CEO Chris Moxham said: “Mayo Clinic is one of the country’s leading centres for ALS care and research, with exceptional clinical expertise and a deep understanding of how the disease progresses in patients.

“We now have the opportunity to connect that clinical depth with molecular data derived directly from patient tissue, giving us a new way to understand the biology of ALS and identify therapeutic targets and potential treatments grounded in patients themselves.”

Headquartered in Palo Alto, California, US, Transcripta Bio is an AI-driven biotechnology company focused on treatments for neurological and neuromuscular illnesses.

Its discovery platform matches disease profiles with opposing compound signatures to identify prospective drugs.

In addition to its ALS research, the company maintains discovery programmes in Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), Facioscapulohumeral Muscular Dystrophy (FSHD), Huntington’s Disease (HD), and Myotonic Dystrophy.

Earlier this year, Merck & Co (MSD) and Mayo Clinic entered a research and development collaboration to utilise AI, advanced analytics, and multimodal clinical data in support of drug discovery and precision medicine.

data.title: Gilead and Vir forge $1.9bn pact to develop next-gen T-cell engagers
data.description:
Gilead Sciences and Vir Biotechnology have deepened their ties by inking a second deal, which will see the pair join forces to discover and engineer novel T-cell engager (TCE) therapies for solid tumours. 

Through this collaboration and licensing agreement, Gilead will hand over $90m upfront and up to $45m in potential near-term preclinical milestones – alongside a potential $1.74bn in further development, regulatory and commercial milestones – in exchange for the exclusive license to develop and commercialise three dual-masked TCEs. The upfront cost includes both $65m in cash and a $25m equity investment. 

This deal will see Gilead hold the power to nominate and advance a trio of therapeutics generated through the partnership, while the pharma giant will also take the helm in developing, manufacturing and potentially commercialising the fruits of this collaboration, which will all target solid tumour-associated antigens. 

At the core of this partnership is Vir’s PRO-XTEN technology, which the company has designed to both extend the half-life of a TCE and prevent the molecule’s activation prior to it reaching the tumour microenvironment.  

Through this mechanism, Vir believes that PRO-XTEN-optimised TCEs could offer improved toxicity and dosing schedule compared with current solid tumour-focused offerings. 

Once Vir develops a TCE, it then employs its artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled dAIsY platform, which the biotech uses to optimise TCEs based on multiple parameters. 

“We believe TCEs have a powerful role to play in the future of immunotherapy to treat cancer,” commented Vir’s president and CEO, Marianne De Backer. 

“This collaboration with Gilead provides an opportunity to generate multiple differentiated candidates aimed at difficult-to-address solid tumours and to expand the potential impact of our science, while also advancing our own clinical oncology portfolio,” De Backer added.  

The latest deal between Gilead and Vir builds on their prior collaborations, which first began in 2021 when the companies joined forces to explore the combinatory potential of their investigational hepatitis B drugs. 

Gilead is not the only pharma player to ink a deal with Vir, however, as the company also recently teamed up with Astellas to co-develop and commercialise VIR-5500, a TCE for prostate cancer in Phase I development. 

TCEs garner big pharma interest across several disease areas 

In recent months, several notable pharma companies have hedged their bets on the potential of TCEs, with companies like GSK, Bristol Myers Squibb (BMS) and UCB all penning deals around the modality over the past year. 

While their roots stem from the blood cancer space, many companies are now exploring their promise further afield, with Gilead recently making its first foray into the TCE arena by outlaying $2.2bn to acquire autoimmune TCE developer Ouro Medicines in March. 

Sanofi and Boehringer Ingelheim have taken a similar tack, with both companies forging deals with Kali Therapeutics and CDR-Life, respectively, to secure the rights to trispecific autoimmune-focused TCEs. 

Meanwhile, analysts at GlobalData, the parent company of Pharmaceutical Technology, recently noted that TCEs are set to disrupt the relapsed and refractory multiple myeloma space in the coming years.

data.title: Rare disease regulation reaches “inflection point” with new FDA framework
data.description:
The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has rolled out a new framework to spur development of new therapies for rare diseases, marking the latest initiative carried out by the Trump administration for the group of disorders.

In a notice via the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), the FDA said the new scheme – dubbed the Rare Disease Framework Initiative – will help “reimagine” development of drugs and biologics for rare diseases.

While the rare disease landscape has seen notable successes in recent decades due to advances in technologies such as gene therapies and disease modelling, there is still a significant gap in approved treatments. According to the HHS, only 5% of rare conditions have an approved treatment.

To spur therapies to market, the FDA outlined several actions it has committed to under the new framework. The agency will provide clearer regulatory decision-making through tailored guidance, improve patient centricity, and better utilise external expertise. The FDA will also apply risk-based approaches, champion use of cutting-edge science, and pool resources and knowledge.

The Initiative is led by the FDA’s Rare Disease Innovation Hub, partnering with the Office of the Commissioner, the Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research (CBER), and the Center for Drug Evaluation and Research (CDER).

The Hub’s director, Amy Comstock Rick, said: “Patients with rare diseases and their families deserve a regulatory process that addresses the uniqueness of each of their conditions while maintaining the FDA’s rigorous standards.

“A bold vision to reimagine the regulatory framework for rare disease drug development that builds on key learnings and milestones is necessary to meet this moment. This new framework will enhance consistency and predictability for both sponsors and for patients.”

Acting FDA commissioner Kyle Diamantas said: “We will remove unnecessary barriers, embrace cutting-edge science, and accelerate promising treatments while upholding FDA’s rigorous standards.”

The National Organization for Rare Disorders (NORD) praised the new framework in a statement, saying the change is an “important and welcome step forward for the rare disease community”.

“What makes this initiative especially important is the opportunity to move beyond case-by-case regulatory accommodations toward a framework designed around the scientific realities of rare diseases,” the non-profit added.

The Rare Foundation, also a non-profit, described the news as “an extraordinary inflection point for the rare disease community.”

US government’s rare disease spotlight

The rollout of the framework marks a continuation of focus on the rare disease space from the Trump administration. In his first term, the President heavily criticised the FDA and its “slow and burdensome” process for bringing innovative therapies to market. Since assuming his second stint at the White House, Trump has overseen several modifications to rare disease regulation via HHS.

In September 2025, the Rare Disease Evidence Principles (RDEP) guidance was introduced to permit certain therapy approvals under one well-controlled clinical study. The Plausible Mechanism Framework shortly followed in November 2025, providing a new pathway to bring ground-breaking personalised therapies to market bypassing traditional requirements, though this still operates as a draft guidance framework.

Then in February 2026, the FDA issued further guidance on accelerating the development of personalised therapies for ultra-rare diseases, specifically highlighting gene-editing and RNA-based approaches.

February also saw the return of the rare paediatric disease priority review voucher (PRV) programme after a lengthy period in legislative limbo. The scheme, which was reinstated via a wider spending bill signed by Trump, acts as a significant incentive for rare disease drug development. Biotechs and rare disease charities have frequently called the PRV programme a vital financial lifeline.

data.title: QCi and INmune Bio partner to study XPro in Alzheimer’s
data.description:
INmune Bio and Quantum Computing, known as QCi, have agreed to collaborate using quantum computing, AI, and data analytics to explore new indications for XPro (XPro1595), an investigational treatment for Alzheimer’s disease and other medical conditions.

The initial agreement marks the first commercial contract in the pharmaceutical and biotechnology sector for QCi.

Under the first stage of the project, the companies will analyse clinical and publicly accessible biomedical datasets to identify conditions sharing the biological mechanisms targeted by XPro.

The agreement also includes options for additional work as clinical programmes progress.

Researchers will combine INmune Bio’s findings from pre-clinical studies and four clinical trials with QCi’s Dirac-3S entropy quantum optimisation machine.

The hardware runs at room temperature and low power, avoiding the specialised cooling systems used by alternative quantum platforms.

The teams will benchmark the quantum machine against standard statistical and machine-learning tools to assess which computational method is best suited for each stage of analysis, while working to build a repeatable discovery model.

INmune Bio CEO David Moss said: “We’ve built a large clinical dataset on Alzheimer’s and other diseases, backed by years of work with XPro. This collaboration allows us to examine patient populations and biomarkers most likely to predict responses by analysing large data sets.

“We’ll look for the diseases with the greatest potential for success, those whose human biology matches what we’ve already seen XPro do, starting with rare diseases where trials can be smaller, faster and more capital-efficient, and where qualifying paediatric approvals may earn a Priority Review Voucher.”

XPro is engineered to neutralise soluble tumour necrosis factor, reducing neuroinflammation whilst preserving protective immune defences.

The therapy holds fast track designation from the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and has completed an End-of-Phase II regulatory meeting, positioning it for an integrated Phase IIb/III trial in early Alzheimer’s disease.

Additionally, INmune Bio is developing CORDStrom, a mesenchymal stromal cell platform for recessive dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa.

Regulatory filings for CORDStrom are scheduled with the UK Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency in 2026, the European Medicines Agency in 2027, and the US FDA.

data.title: ImmunityBio’s bladder cancer drug, Anktiva lands US label expansion
data.description:
The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has awarded a label expansion to ImmunityBio-owned Altor Bioscience’s bladder cancer therapy, Anktiva (nogapendekin alfa inbakicept-pmln), three months ahead of its original PDUFA date, making it the first drug approved for patients with high-grade papillary-only disease.  

Following the FDA’s blessing, US patients with BCG-unresponsive high-grade, papillary-only non-muscle invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC) can now receive treatment with the interleukin-15 receptor agonist. This extends the use case for Anktiva, which was first approved in 2024 alongside the Bacillus Calmette–Guérin (BCG) vaccine for the treatment of patients with BCG-unresponsive NMIBC with carcinoma in situ (CIS). 

Anktiva’s expanded approval stems from the positive outcomes of the Phase III QUILT-3.032 study (NCT03022825) in which the drug triggered a 62% complete response (CR) rate in the FDA-label population, with 40% of these individuals maintaining their response at the 24-month mark.  

It also marks a change in tack strategy-wise for the FDA’s review of NMIBC drugs, as the agency primarily leaned on data that had led to Anktiva’s earlier approval in a separate patient population.  

According to Dr R. Angelo de Claro, director of the FDA’s Oncology Center of Excellence, this was made possible through the regulator’s review of clinical and laboratory evidence, which proved the similarities between carcinoma in situ (CIS) and the high-grade papillary-only NMIBC. Because of this overlap, the FDA was able to use data from patients with CIS pathology to inform its decision. 

This approach, Claro says, could also potentially help guide the development of future treatments in NMIBC. To support this, the agency is currently working on finalising a draft guidance on developing drugs for BCG-unresponsive NMIBC, which aims to lay out a framework for sponsors who want to use evidence from patients with CIS to support potential approvals for individuals with high-grade, papillary-only disease. 

Analysts tout Anktiva’s ‘first-mover’ advantage

Anktiva’s expanded approval in NMIBC gives it a leg-up on its current competitors in the BCG-unresponsive patient population, as it is now the only drug to have secured the regulatory green light specifically for the treatment of high-grade papillary-only cases.  

According to Jefferies analysts, Anktiva’s new label expansion could double the current addressable NIMBC population as a first mover, while “setting a regulatory precedent for competitors.” They add that the drug’s on-label approval will also “broaden use beyond early adopters and may improve commercial payer coverage.”

The FDA had originally requested ImmunityBio to run a separate Phase III trial for expansion into this indication, but the pair later agreed this would not be required. Johnson & Johnson, however, is already running a Phase III trial, the Sunrise-5 study, of its NMIBC therapy Inlexzo (gemcitabine intravesical system) after it was also told by the agency this was required for an expansion into high-grade papillary-only cases. 

Currently, there are only a few on-patent drugs approved to treat the BCG-unresponsive subset of NMIBC patients with CIS, including Ferring Pharmaceuticals’ gene therapy, Adstiladrin (nadofaragene firadenovec‐vncg), MSD’s Keytruda (pembrolizumab) and Inlexzo. 

Currently, GlobalData, parent company of Pharmaceutical Technology, estimates that Anktiva will reach blockbuster status in 2029, while going on to generate north of $4bn in global sales for ImmunityBio in 2032.

data.title: Alentis and PinotBio partner to develop claudin-1 oncology ADCs
data.description:
Alentis Therapeutics and PinotBio have entered into a research collaboration and licensing agreement to develop claudin-1-targeting antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) for oncology indications.

Under the agreement, Alentis has secured an exclusive option to in-license linkers and payloads from PinotBio for use in its pipeline candidates.

Financially, PinotBio will receive an upfront payment alongside eligibility for development, regulatory, and commercial milestone payments.

Alentis will also pay royalties on net sales for any therapy candidate it chooses to commercialise.

The partnership aims to apply PinotBio’s platform technologies to Alentis’ antibody assets to address claudin-1, a target expressed across more than ten tumour types.

Alentis Therapeutics CEO Dr Mark Pruzanski said: “Claudin-1 continues to gain recognition as a highly promising target and, together with our partner PinotBio, we aim to further expand its therapeutic potential and maximise patient benefit across a range of high-unmet need cancers.

“This expanded relationship builds on our successful research collaboration, during which we explored dozens of ADC constructs and saw firsthand the strength of PinotBio’s science and execution.”

Alentis is currently assessing two clinical-stage oncology conjugates in Phase I/II trials across solid tumours expressing claudin-1: ALE.P02, which carries a tubulin inhibitor payload, and ALE.P03, which uses a topoisomerase I inhibitor payload.

The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) granted fast track designation to ALE.P02 for advanced or metastatic claudin-1-positive squamous tumours.

Additionally, Alentis is evaluating lixudebart in a Phase Ib trial for advanced liver fibrosis and a Phase II study in anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA)-associated vasculitis with renal involvement.

The company has partnered with Commonwealth Serum Laboratories (CSL) to co-develop and co-promote the antibody for conditions including associated vasculitis with rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (AAV-RPGN), focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS), and primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC).

Alentis was founded on research conducted in France at the University of Strasbourg and Inserm.

Headquartered in South Korea and founded in 2017, PinotBio focuses on therapies for recurrent and resistant disease. Four programmes currently use its PINOT-ADC platform: CT-P70, CT-P71, CT-P73, and PBX-004.

The three partnered candidates being developed with Celltrion have received US FDA Fast Track designation, whilst PBX-004 remains wholly owned. PinotBio’s institutional backers include IMM Investment and KB Investment.
